title: The Psychology of Learning from Machines: Anthropomorphic AI and the Paradox of Automation in Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines the psychology of learning from anthropomorphic AI in education, asking what prior research from automation psychology, human factors, HCI, and philosophy of technology can tell us about how learners relate to AI tutors. The authors focus on three central problems intensified by generative AI: trust calibration failures (both automation bias and algorithm aversion), the risks of anthropomorphic design, and the persistence of automation ironies in which systems intended to support learning may weaken human skill and judgment.

The study uses a dual approach. First, it provides a cross-disciplinary theoretical synthesis across five research traditions. Second, it conducts an empirical analysis of YouTube discourse, comparing comments on AI-generated philosophical debate videos with comments on human-created engineering tutorial videos. The dataset includes 104,984 comments total, with sentiment analysis, engagement profiling, temporal analysis, and qualitative coding of a 300-comment subsample. Rather than testing a classroom intervention, the paper analyzes naturalistic audience responses to AI-generated educational content and uses these patterns to derive implications for educational AI design.

No specific student participant population is directly reported, since the empirical component is based on public online comments rather than a defined educational cohort. The context is online, centered on YouTube educational media and broader implications for engineering education. The authors argue that trust in AI is domain-dependent: audiences are more accepting of AI for abstract or structured content but become polarized on moral and ethical topics. They also find strong anthropomorphic projection toward AI despite minimal cues, while noting that human-created engineering tutorials elicit more gratitude and parasocial teacher-like responses than AI-generated debates.

The paper concludes that AI should be deployed in a differentiated and complementary way in education. It recommends AI support for well-structured, convergent, foundational technical tasks, while preserving human leadership for ethics, design judgment, professional identity formation, and emotionally or relationally significant aspects of learning. The authors propose design principles including transparency about AI limitations, calibrated anthropomorphism, scaffolding that preserves learner agency and productive struggle, and safeguards against inappropriate personhood conferral or emotional dependency.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI and anthropomorphic AI tutors/chatbots with conversational interfaces used as educational supports or content generators, rather than a specific named product.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper develops a theoretical framework for how learners relate psychologically to anthropomorphic AI tutors and AI-generated educational content, supported by naturalistic analysis of YouTube comments on AI-generated philosophical debates versus human-created engineering tutorials.

quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a theoretical synthesis/framework paper with an exploratory observational discourse analysis of YouTube comments. It does not evaluate a specific educational AI intervention on student learning outcomes in a controlled design.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for meaningful psychological and pedagogical risks and differentiated uses of GenAI, but it does not report direct causal effect sizes on student outcomes for the focal tool studied here.
